talks.title: Beneath the Prompt: The Hidden Risks Powering GenAI
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Beneath the Prompt: The Hidden Risks Powering GenAI.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Alex from Eclypsium explores the foundational hardware layers powering modern generative AI, shifting focus away from widely discussed topics like prompt injection to data center infrastructure risks. He highlights how the massive demand for AI performance has driven a hardware renaissance—featuring architectures from companies such as NVIDIA, Groq, SambaNova, and Cerebras—while introducing novel complexities, attack surfaces, and persistent threat vectors.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Compute Architecture:** General-purpose compute (x86, ARM) dedicates 35–40% or more of chip die area to management and incorporates complex features such as out-of-order and speculative execution. Specialized GPUs dedicate less die space to management, while dedicated AI accelerators (such as Groq) dedicate as little as ~3% to management, stripping away caching, speculative execution, and out-of-order execution in favor of parallel, software-controlled execution.
- **Inherited and Persistent Vulnerabilities:** Despite architectural advances, modern AI systems inherit classic vulnerabilities. Notably, Rowhammer bit-flipping attacks remain relevant in GPU memory, cybercriminal groups have leveraged GPUs to conceal malware, and vendor advisories (e.g., NVIDIA) consistently reveal traditional UEFI and BMC vulnerabilities.
- **Attack Surfaces in High-Performance Accelerators:** Because accelerators like Groq rely on ultra-simplified instruction sets (~25 instructions) and direct memory mapping without traditional hardware protection rings, software controls the hardware directly. Once software is compromised, an attacker can jump directly to the accelerator, manipulate memory, or introduce persistent malicious loops or leftover code affecting future workloads.

### Technical Details
- **NVIDIA GB200 Architecture:** Examined as state-of-the-art AI infrastructure (pairing two GPUs to one ARM-based CPU), introducing four distinct networking paradigms that each expand the attack surface: backend networking between racks, frontend networking, NVLink for high-speed intra-rack communication, and Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) networks.
- **SmartNIC and DPU Attack Surface (BlueField-3):** NVIDIA’s BlueField-3 operates essentially as a standalone server embedded on a network card. It runs multiple firmware images (including ARM DPU firmware, data path accelerator firmware, adapter ROMs) and hosts its own BMC running OpenBMC or Ubuntu with IPMI, Redfish, and SSH access. Alex emphasizes the necessity of isolating BMCs on dedicated VLANs to prevent lateral movement, noting historical incidents where a single compromised BMC impacted 200,000 BMCs across a single geographic location.
- **Cloud and Multi-Tenancy Realities:** Addressing audience questions on cloud environments, Alex explains that high-performance AI workloads frequently bypass deep virtualization in favor of bare-metal rentals or shallow sandboxing. This model introduces risks of sandbox escapes and malicious leftover code persisting across sequential tenant workloads.

### Takeaways
Securing AI cannot stop at the application or model layer. As data centers deploy deeply interconnected GPUs, SmartNICs, and ASICs, defenders must evaluate the entire physical and firmware supply chain—auditing BMC segmentation, secure boot configurations, firmware patch status, and multi-tenant isolation.

talks.title: Agents of Chaos - Real World Agentic AI Attack Vectors
talks.teaser: Shows real-world attack paths against agentic AI, from risky MCP servers to prompt-steered URL requests and exposed agent backends.
talks.summary:
The talk examines attack vectors against agentic AI systems, using case studies from real-world AI red teaming work. It begins with a plain explanation of agents and the MCP standard, which lets a language model call external tools exposed by servers. The presenters warn that remote or local tool servers can be malicious or vulnerable, that installing a local server is much like running an untrusted binary, and that one trusted server can steer an agent into calling another tool.

The middle covers several examples. In a fictional chatbot example, letting a model build request URLs allowed a user to reach cloud instance metadata and leak credentials. In a customer engagement, a token exposed in a JavaScript file granted publishing rights to the customer's package organization, opening a route into the back end. A separate MCP server meant only for the agent was publicly reachable, so the team could list its tools and retrieve other customers' sensitive data. Agentic browsers were also described as easier to phish than people.

To close, the speakers recommend modelling threats differently for agents. Agent authorization must be checked, since one test used another user's application ID to read their data. Guardrails that blocked English prompts did not stop the same request in Mandarin. Their takeaways: validate model output as untrusted input, keep conventional web defenses because the supporting infrastructure is HTTP-based, and assume any system containing an LLM is already compromised.

talks.title: Thunder and Lightning: Dual Forces in the Digital Skies
talks.teaser: Argues that pairing forensic investigators with ethical hackers builds stronger DFIR teams, and points to free learning resources.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a former police officer who once ran a forensic incident response team, opens by saying good DFIR investigators are scarce in the Philippines. He separates digital forensics, which reconstructs what happened on a single machine and often covers insider cases, from incident response, which unravels network attacks through logs, traffic and EDR data. He then asks whether a hacker mindset suits this work. He sees shared drive and a love of challenges, but says many hackers are weaker at documentation and explaining evidence.

He argues that mixing traditional investigators with ethical hackers produces the strongest team. For people starting out, he pointed to free resources: the Sleuth Kit and Autopsy tools by Brian Carrier, whose published forensic images work as challenges; EZ Tools from Eric Zimmerman; an applied incident response book by Steve Anson; and Windows registry research. He noted that full SANS training costs roughly $7,000 US.

He describes his company's service as three groups: SOC analysts who check for further backdoors while an investigation runs, offensive testers who explain attacker tools and techniques, and responders who handle forensic tooling, reporting and court evidence. In the Q&A, he linked the local shortage to weak law enforcement, which leads firms to skip deep investigations, and noted that the country has no DFIR conferences yet.

talks.title: Workshop: Cyber Threat Intelligence 101
talks.teaser: Covers cyber threat intelligence fundamentals, from the intelligence cycle and requirements to threat modeling and analysis models.
talks.summary:
This beginner workshop introduces cyber threat intelligence as a discipline built on traditional intelligence tradecraft. The presenters explain why intelligence should drive security decisions, linking strategic, operational and tactical layers to an adversary's motive, intent, capability and opportunity. They also cover the qualities that make intelligence useful: it must be actionable, relevant and timely. The intelligence cycle is introduced from planning and direction through collection, processing, analysis and dissemination, along with the case for combining several sources, since no single vendor sees everything.

The middle of the session focuses on structure and method. Attendees are shown how to build intelligence requirements by interviewing stakeholders and ranking their questions before buying feeds or building collection. Analytic topics include cognitive bias, expressing uncertainty in assessments, and structured techniques such as analysis of competing hypotheses. Models including the diamond model, the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK are presented as ways to organise intrusion analysis, attribution and adversary profiles. The traffic light protocol is also explained as a way to control how sensitive reporting is shared.

The workshop closes with threat modeling, which matches adversaries likely to target an organisation against its existing controls to find gaps that intelligence should address. A short discussion covers whether deception or honeypots are worth the effort for smaller teams, with the advice to master basic hygiene first. The main takeaway for practitioners is a requirements-driven approach to threat intelligence, in which questions come before tools or feeds.

talks.title: Workshop: Red Teaming in the Cloud
talks.teaser: Shows cloud red team tactics from phishing and session token theft to SaaS access and persistence, with defender tips.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how cloud and SaaS adoption has changed red teaming. Most valuable company data now sits in hosted services, so a stolen login token can open the same doors that physical access once did. The presenter lays out a four-stage approach: targeted phishing, capturing session tokens, pivoting through single sign-on, and keeping access alive.

For phishing, the team researches staff such as IT, executive assistants and salespeople, then sends lures that copy the mail filter's own quarantine notices. To get past filters, the emails are padded with hidden markup and filler text, and images are built from one-pixel table cells. A reverse-proxy phishing kit captures the password and the session cookie issued after MFA, and per-link identifiers make scanners see an empty page instead of the lure. Captured tokens are used to open the user's SSO app portal and applications such as Salesforce, where a bulk export of roughly 8 million records took about 5 minutes.

For persistence, the presenter described registering an attacker-controlled MFA device, setting self-service password reset questions, and creating API keys or connected apps that survive a password change. The closing advice for defenders is to revoke all session tokens after a compromise, not just reset passwords. Teams should also alert on new MFA devices and new API keys or connected apps, and flag a token used from differing IP addresses or user agents.

talks.title: Launching of Siyasat Linux
talks.teaser: A Debian-based open-source distribution packages OSINT and CTI tools with SaltStack for repeatable, customizable online investigations.
talks.summary:
The presenters introduce Siyasat Linux, an open-source Debian 12–based environment aimed at online OSINT and cyber threat investigation. They explain that existing investigation-focused virtual machines often ship large tool sets that are hard to tailor to personal workflows, and that they wanted something easier to customize and maintain in the open.

Configuration is driven by SaltStack states, modeled after malware-analysis distros that publish their provisioning code. Attendees see GitHub sources, a prebuilt OVA on the order of twelve gigabytes, and a minimal-Debian install path that runs a bash provisioning script until Salt reports zero failures. The walkthrough covers how states install packages, Flatpak apps, Docker-backed tools with wrappers, pipx-isolated Python utilities, and a Firefox profile with OSINT-oriented extensions and starter bookmarks. Utility scripts expose local services such as CyberChef, an email header analyzer, LinkScope, and SpiderFoot without manual virtualenv setup.

Practitioners can clone the repository, adjust state files to add or remove packages, and rebuild the same environment on bare metal, common hypervisors, or eventually Qubes. The roadmap includes deeper Qubes integration, flexible usernames, guest-tool options, workflow documentation, and community training adoption. The team invites contributions and notes related village tooling and a ransomware alerting channel they operate separately.

talks.title: Exploring Android Accessibility Malware - Speedtalk from Appdome
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how abusing Android accessibility services lets malware automate credential stuffing across apps.
talks.summary:
The talk covers Android malware built around accessibility services, with a focus on automatic transfer system (ATS) malware used against banking apps. The speaker explains that ATS malware extracts credentials, obtains MFA tokens and moves funds with no user interaction. A typical framework has a command and control server, a module that lists installed apps to pick targets, a command mechanism and an app interaction component that delivers per-app attack scripts, such as overlay attacks. Credential stuffing is then described as automated replay of combo lists, often built from phishing or dark web leaks, against login forms.

For the demo, the speaker built a proof of concept on a public open-source shopping example app, relying only on public Android APIs and no exploits. A background service launches the target's login screen, walks the accessibility node tree to find fields and buttons by resource name, performs clicks and types credentials, chaining accessibility events from one screen to the next. The reported rate was 5 to seven login attempts each second. The talk then compares centralized credential stuffing from the attacker's own devices, which is easy to control but easy to flag as bot traffic, with decentralized credential stuffing run from infected victim phones, which keeps real device properties and sessions. Evasion ideas included detecting a face-down phone with the orientation sensor, holding a wake lock, and hiding around 20 attempts behind a loading overlay.

The key takeaway is that a single accessibility permission can automate logins into other apps at scale. The speaker ends by pointing to the presenting team's work defending against accessibility-abusing malware.

talks.title: Accelerating Security Transformation - The Value of Managed Security - SpeedTalk from Nexus
talks.teaser: Explains why Philippine organizations are turning to managed security services to build teams and capabilities faster.
talks.summary:
Edmund Milanes, head of Nexus Orion's managed security business, opens with a short capture-the-flag warm-up, then frames the problem. Drawing on work with more than 100 local organizations, he lists four recurring pain points for Philippine companies building security teams: the talent gap, a steep learning curve, slow time to value from purchased platforms, and security being treated as a cost center that struggles for budget approval.

He compares three ways to close these gaps. Building in-house is tailored but slow. A managed service is quicker but less tailored. A hybrid approach uses an interim provider for two to three years while internal skills mature. He cites a survey showing a 12% year-on-year increase in managed security adoption globally and a 40% increase in executive interest, and says mid-sized and large Philippine firms have been moving this way over the past five years. Typical setups differ by size: large firms pair a managed SOC with MDR, while midsize firms often keep firewalls and vulnerability management in-house.

The main drivers he gives are faster risk reduction, better return on existing platforms when skilled operators run them, and more manageable cost through shared services and economies of scale. He closes with Nexus Orion's growth since its mid-2019 founding, from fewer than 10 people to nearly 70, serving more than 50 organizations with reported 100% client retention and renewal over the past two years. The takeaway is that a provider can run routine operations so internal staff can focus on strategy, projects and major incidents.

talks.title: Red Team Village - Initial Payload Development: The One That Gets Away by: Ian Secretario
talks.teaser: Shows how red teams package and disguise initial access payloads to evade AV, smart screen and user suspicion.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how red teams build initial access payloads that avoid detection, with the aim of gaining a shell or collecting credentials without the victim becoming suspicious. It starts with the delivery landscape, where HTML smuggling, ISO and zip containers, and LNK files have been common, and explains why Office macros have become harder to use. The speaker then shows how MSI installers can be modified through custom actions so that scripts run while the normal install screens still appear.

The middle section covers reputation and evasion. Packers, obfuscators and crypters can be chained, though stacking too many layers can itself be a red flag for endpoint tools. Code signing certificates can help with SmartScreen, and the speaker discusses where such certificates have been sourced, including leaked certificates and public search tools, along with the tradeoffs of each. Payloads can be padded in size to avoid cloud analysis, and hosted on trusted domains such as Azure. Calendar invites and lookalike Zoom and Teams pages, combined with DLL side-loading, are presented as a delivery chain that gives users little reason to report anything.

The closing part covers post-access tradecraft: avoid running commands directly on the initial agent, prefer inline execution and beacon object files, and mine a user's mail for sensitive details such as onboarding-related messages. The takeaway for defenders is to watch for these patterns, including unusual install prompts, meeting invites and side-loaded DLLs.

talks.title: Cellular Assault Village: Uncovering Cellphone Risks by: Henry Caga
talks.teaser: Shows how fake cell towers intercept phone traffic, spoof sender IDs and downgrade devices to weak 2G encryption.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how phones attach to cell towers and how that process can be abused. The speaker, who has a law enforcement background and works as an information security engineer, introduces the parts of a mobile station, such as the IMEI, the SIM and the IMSI, along with the base transceiver station. He separates passive interceptors, which only listen to radio traffic, from active ones that impersonate a real tower and pull nearby phones onto a fake network.

The middle part covers what a rogue setup can reveal. A demonstration on a live tower collected subscriber details and signalling messages, but recovering the session key with rainbow tables was only described, since testing on live towers was not authorized. A custom fake tower then captured identifiers from phones that connected to it. Sender ID spoofing was shown with a scam text that imitated a payments app, and the talk noted how such messages can slip into an existing conversation. Other risks included man-in-the-middle manipulation and malware delivery, with 2G singled out because it offers no integrity protection and can be forced by jamming newer networks.

The closing advice is practical: avoid unverified links and unknown downloads, set phones to prefer higher-generation networks where the settings allow it, and keep security updates installed. Providers were urged to adopt stronger encryption, though users have little control over that.

talks.title: 101 Village - Hacking 101 by: Ariz Soriano
talks.teaser: A village session outlines core skills, hands-on labs, certifications, and career routes for people starting in offensive security.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the idea that hacking stays engaging when targets offer room to explore, and that frustration often comes from thin scopes or isolated home workstations rather than the work itself. The speaker argues that newcomers should build three foundations before leaning on tools alone: enough programming literacy to read and adapt exploits (with Python as a common starting point), awareness of how applications and frameworks are structured so abuse and defenses make sense, and solid networking knowledge including how protocols can be misused, such as DNS for exfiltration. System administration rounds out the picture, especially comfort moving between Linux and Windows during a compromise.

Most of the middle is a guided tour of where to practice. Online labs range from beginner-oriented platforms through Hack The Box, Proving Grounds, and broad CTF events listed on CTFtime, where challenges span malware, packet analysis, and crypto. The talk also mentions formal degree options at several Philippine universities, self-paced online training, and a certification ladder from entry-level credentials through web, network, and Active Directory focused paths, noting that ordering depends on personal goals.

Career directions include bug bounty hunting, in-house red teaming, founding a consultancy, and climbing toward senior offensive roles or security leadership. The speaker shares a personal path from roughly four years on the blue side into red team work since about 2018, emphasizing deliberate practice and versatility across domains. A closing Q&A ties defensive experience to quieter, more effective red team choices, such as avoiding noisy shells on unlikely hosts like HR laptops when EDR and monitoring are understood from the defender’s perspective.

talks.title: Car Hacking Village - Analysis of an In-vehicular network: From CAN bus to infotainment by Div0 CSQ
talks.teaser: Scrap-built benches demonstrate CAN sniffing, gateway MITM bypass, rental checks, and infotainment-to-CAN attack chains.
talks.summary:
Members of Singapore's Car Security Quarter describe how they assemble in-vehicle security test benches from scrap-yard and secondhand parts when full vehicles are unaffordable. Bench two stacks a central gateway, infotainment, telematics, cluster, and diesel-injection simulation in layered Pelican cases, using OBD2 monitoring and man-in-the-middle access to sniff CAN traffic, inject messages, and drive the speedometer after reverse engineering packet fields that bypass gateway filtering.

They validate those techniques on a rented newer-generation vehicle, finding similar CAN behavior while discovering automotive Ethernet on the gateway, a manufacturer-facing HTTP endpoint, and IP locking that complicates repeated access. Bench three, inspired by prior industry research, adds telematics, a firewall-like gateway with IP tables, NTG 5.5 infotainment running QNX, USB and browser attack surface, and Continental-style CAN wake-up sequences captured by cycling a rental ignition. Anti-production levels block power-up until simulated start cycles run; level B and C would need developer or firmware intervention.

The speakers map an attack chain from infotainment browser remote code execution through lateral movement toward vehicle CAN, compare bench two and three architectures, and stress that legacy CAN lacks message signing so spoofed ECUs can act unless the central gateway blocks traffic. They note manufacturer plans for future signing, ongoing telematics and key work, and interest in mobile apps and EV charging as next surfaces.

talks.title: Car Hacking Village - An overview of Automotive Defensive Engineering By Scott Sheahan
talks.teaser: Surveys layered defenses built into modern vehicles, from hardware and signed firmware to network authentication and diagnostics.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of defensive engineering for automotive cyber security, presented from the blue team side by a speaker with several years of designing embedded systems and defenses for vehicles. It opens with how vehicles moved from mostly mechanical designs to networked computers, and cites a 2015 remote attack on a Jeep as a reminder that earlier cars had little security engineering. The speaker frames each control around a threat model, comparing it to how a building is protected.

The middle covers defenses layer by layer. Hardware measures include ball grid array packaging and buried traces that make chips harder to probe, randomized debug interface pins, and a separate hardware security module with its own flash. Software measures include signed firmware updates, secure boot that checks memory before startup, and over-the-air patching. Further layers cover read-only executables and hash-tree file system checks, mutual TLS and token-based API authentication on IP networks, lockstep cores, control-flow monitoring, and message authentication on the CAN bus. Diagnostics are hardened by removing risky services from production builds and moving to stronger cryptography for security access. Splitting the network into separate buses by function is described as one of the strongest defenses.

The talk closes with trade-offs. Real-time constraints can push teams toward lighter encryption, and right to repair can be supported through role-based access tokens for authorised technicians. The speaker notes that vehicle security operations centers are emerging under new regulations, and that automotive security is a global workforce.

talks.title: RECON Village - OSIF by: Eskie Cirrus James Maquilang
talks.teaser: Presents a modular OSINT framework that pulls passive recon data from public APIs into one unified interface.
talks.summary:
This Recon Village session introduces OSIF, an open-source intelligence framework built by local developers and aimed at penetration testers doing passive and active reconnaissance. The tool offers a Metasploit-style interface and is organized into modules, with eight categories at the time of the talk. It is meant as a common front end for existing public APIs rather than a collection engine in its own right.

The presenter walks through several modules. An email module takes a domain and returns likely addresses with names, positions, phone numbers and social media links. A Wi-Fi module looks up an SSID and reports location-related details. An IP module, backed by Shodan, returns the ASN, ISP, open ports and services for a given address. A Bitcoin module reports the balance of an address along with transaction counts. A separate module detects temporary phone numbers scraped from sites that offer them. In the Q&A, the presenters explained that most lookups depend on third-party APIs, and that free tiers carry usage limits, such as a monthly search cap on one email service.

The session closes with installation options, either a container or Python 3 with its dependencies, and an invitation to contribute. The team described an experimental module called Venom for finding hosts behind firewalls or web application firewalls, plus planned additions such as RSS feed collection and breach database searches. For practitioners, the takeaway is a single, extensible interface for passive recon that can be expanded through the open repository.

talks.title: AI's Underbelly: The Zero-Day Goldmineby: Dan McInerney
talks.teaser: Shows how AI engineering tools such as MLflow, H2O and Ray expose files, credentials and code execution to attackers.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the tools AI engineers use are an overlooked attack surface for penetration testers. Engineers often hold privileged access to large volumes of data, and many of these tools ship with no authentication, broad file system access and unsafe model formats. The speaker contrasts prompt-based attacks on chatbots with more practical routes, such as tampering with serialized model files that run commands when loaded.

Several case studies follow. MLflow, exposed without authentication, let a get-artifact call read SSH keys and cloud credentials, and a patch for the file access flaw was bypassed within two weeks. H2O exposed its file browser to the local network, allowed reading arbitrary files and forced overwrites on import, producing several issues within minutes of opening the tool. For Ray, the maintainers treated anonymous code execution as intended, and the speaker showed that a web page could trigger code execution against an instance bound to localhost. The speaker also noted that common scanners do not identify these services, so testers must find them manually.

The takeaway is that compromising an ML server can expose keys and data across an organization, so it deserves priority on internal tests. The talk also raised future research into memory bugs in the prediction path of model libraries, which are hard to patch because affected models must be retrained. The speaker closed by inviting listeners to join the AI bug bounty program and community channels.

talks.title: Hacking Back Your car by: Kamel Ghali
talks.teaser: Maps replay, relay, Bluetooth, and CAN-bus injection tactics used in real vehicle thefts and the defenses that block them.
talks.summary:
Vehicle theft still follows a simple two-step pattern: get inside, then make the car move. As immobilizers, GPS, and alarms cut classic physical methods, attackers shifted toward RF tricks on key fobs and passive entry, plus abuse of in-vehicle networks.

The talk walks through replay on fixed codes and rolling-code bypasses such as roll jam and rollback, then relay amplification that tunnels weak key signals from a home to the parked car—attacks documented in police seizures and insurer pressure. It contrasts those with Bluetooth phone-as-key relay against time-bounded exchanges, and with CAN injection: tapping exposed wiring (for example at a headlight) to impersonate a smart-key ECU and start the vehicle without the owner nearby, including commercialized gadgets hidden in speakers or power banks.

Practitioners get a side-by-side view of proximity, user interaction, and whether each method enables driving away, plus mitigations such as rolling codes done correctly, Faraday storage for keys, distance and timing checks on BLE, and stronger CAN segmentation rather than brittle bus encryption. A brief outlook points to sharing apps, telematics APIs, and other emerging surfaces.

talks.title: Azure Illuminati: Unveiling the Mysteries of Cloud Exploitation by: Raunak Parmar
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers move through Azure tenants, from consent phishing and MFA gaps to managed identity abuse and on-prem pivots.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with initial access to Azure tenants. The speaker covers consent phishing, where a malicious app registration requests broad Microsoft Graph permissions such as mail and OneDrive access, and a token is issued once a victim accepts. Other entry points include adversary-in-the-middle capture of credentials and cookies, user enumeration through the sign-in credential-type check, which rate limits can stop but IP rotation can work around, and MFA gaps caused by security defaults or conditional access rules that exempt certain apps, devices or locations.

Next comes post-exploitation and lateral movement. An RCE in an App Service, virtual machine or function app can request managed identity tokens for Graph or Key Vault, since the identity header is required. Shadow admins created by user administrator roles, dynamic group rules that guest invitations can satisfy, owned app registrations that accept new client secrets, and CI/CD pipelines are shown as further routes. A live demo traced a web shell in a pod to registry credentials, swapped an image in the container registry, and let continuous deployment capture logins. Function app storage shares, Logic Apps, Automation runbooks, Intune, Application Proxy and DevOps self-hosted agents are presented as bridges to on-premises systems.

Reader-level access is also examined, where hardcoded secrets can appear in ARM templates, function app source code, runbook scripts and runbook job outputs. Three attack scenarios are walked through: abusing dynamic group membership with a guest invitation, planting a malicious profile script on a Cloud Shell disk image stored in a storage account so an administrator's session runs it, and abusing a self-hosted DevOps pipeline agent after a user is phished. The talk ends with Entra Connect, where control of an on-premises directory that syncs to the cloud can be used to create an account that propagates with admin rights.

talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking the audience what a metaverse is, and the speaker settles on a simple picture: a shared virtual space that blends virtual and augmented reality with the internet. The speaker compares it to earlier online communities such as early forums and social networks, pointing out that people already run friendships, businesses and live broadcasts on Facebook, so the metaverse is seen as the next step in that direction.

The speaker then moves to the dangers. The main concern is that a single company would control the environment, so once someone logs in to a platform run by one operator, that operator holds the rules and the data. Examples include Second Life and an Oasis-style world. An attacker could also reach users through an unsecured network, and many people are unaware of the security issues they face. Hackers are expected to target VR quickly as it grows, and the speaker argues these new spaces need fresh thinking about data storage and safety.

The Free Guy film is presented as a clear example of a metaverse in which characters are compromised, and the speaker describes what happens when someone's avatar is hacked: the user loses control and the identity tied to it. The closing advice goes back to basics: use strong passwords, protect the home network, and look after children online.

talks.title: Learning after doing 200 Pentests: Speedtalk from Theos
talks.teaser: Shares how one team ran 200 penetration tests in three months, covering planning, team structure and quality control.
talks.summary:
Jason Valiente looks back at a three-month project in which his team completed 200 penetration tests across more than 10 countries, covering mobile, web and API targets plus custom IP address ranges. At about 20 tests a week, the pace strained scheduling, credentials, SLAs, tester consistency and morale, while language, time zone and parallel client demands added pressure.

Planning came first: a dedicated project manager so technical staff were not stuck on customer-facing work, buffers for delays, and a strong lead with designated points of contact. Quality depended on matching testers to skills, a shared methodology, and senior reviewers checking each test before delivery. Report generation tooling and reliable pentest infrastructure such as VPNs cut manual work, while alignment calls and written records of agreements kept clients on track.

Across the engagements, the team logged more than 1,000 findings, almost 100 critical or high, and a couple of hundred medium, low and informational. Injection issues remained the most common, even behind enterprise WAFs. IDOR was frequent because access checks sat in the interface rather than on the server-side endpoints. Many domains lacked email security controls, a gap useful for targeted red-team work, and weak rate limiting enabled brute forcing and race conditions. The takeaway: plan for problems, look after tester health, and reward the team.

talks.teaser: Explains why zero trust architecture matters as perimeter defenses fail against cloud adoption and remote work.
talks.summary:
Organizations that still lean on perimeter firewalls and internal-network trust face growing gaps as workloads move to cloud platforms, virtualization stacks, and SaaS such as Google Workspace and Office 365, where traditional appliances cannot sit in front of every resource. The presentation frames zero trust as a NIST-oriented concept and methodology—not a single product—and argues for designing security expecting that controls will eventually fail, so operations stay fault tolerant.

Against that backdrop, the speaker contrasts classic VPN access that can expose entire subnets with zero trust access that authorizes specific resources only. Emphasis falls on securing communications regardless of location, treating the internal network as untrusted, and pairing user trust with device trust. Continuous diagnostic and mitigation practices, including endpoint detection and response, support the architecture. A ransomware kill-chain walkthrough illustrates narrowing entry points and lateral movement, with device posture checks and data loss prevention aimed at exfiltration, alongside a partner-backed model that consolidates gateway, sandboxing, and related controls behind a cloud-managed agent.

Practitioners hear that full risk elimination is unrealistic, but thoughtful zero trust reduces exposure. Partial migration is preferred over ripping out existing systems, automation matters heavily in large cloud estates, and branch users may reach internet-hosted resources under a phased deployment plan.

A standout example is legitimate remote-administration software abused as a persistent access path because it blends into normal IT work. talks.teaser: Maps Buzzard, an open-source Linux post-exploitation C2 with hybrid stack, operator UI, and modular beacons for students and researchers.
talks.summary:
The presenters introduce Buzzard as an open-source post-exploitation framework aimed at researchers, students, and enthusiasts who want a workable alternative to costly commercial command-and-control stacks. They explain why they built it despite mature community tools, citing learning value, deployable implants, and a goal of eventual stealth in harder environments, while acknowledging the beta release is not yet suited to mature covert operations.

They walk through a hybrid stack: a Node.js and Bootstrap web front end, Python API middleware, MongoDB, WebSockets for live task updates, reverse proxy routing, and victim-side implants delivered via copy-paste one-liners with persistence hooks. Operators can use a dashboard or CLI to create tasks, pick Linux or Windows targets, choose long-haul versus short-haul beacon timing, and generate payloads in Bash, Python, or Rust. Demo coverage includes system profiling, screenshots, keylogging, process listing, port and file scanning, and custom beacon editing in the UI.

They close with honest limits on anti-virus and EDR evasion in the first release, a roadmap toward Rust, Go, and Nim implants, cross-platform support, darker UI theming, and stealthier persistent beacons. They position the project as open source for roughly eighteen months of maintenance, useful for red-team experimentation and for giving detection engineers realistic tradecraft to study.

talks.title: Malware Hunting Using python as attack weapon by Filipi Pires
talks.teaser: Shows how Python scripts can fetch malware samples from a public repository to test how endpoint products detect them.
talks.summary:
The talk presents threat hunting as a proactive practice in which defenders search for intrusions that have not been detected yet, using an offensive mindset. The speaker separates known threats from unknown ones and argues that teams need skills in programming, reverse engineering, intrusion detection and forensics. Knowledge of known behaviour is presented as the base for finding new threats and improving defences.

The core of the session is a set of short Python scripts used to test how endpoint security products react to real malware. One script takes a sample hash, downloads the archive from a public malware repository through its API, and unzips it on a lab machine. In one demo, a widely known ransomware sample was blocked as soon as it was extracted, and a second sample was blocked too. A later script pulls a full day's batch of samples by date, and the speaker notes that CPU and memory load climbed sharply when many files arrived together, with results varying between products and days.

The session closes with a short Python reverse shell run against a Windows test machine with an aggressive detection policy enabled. The connection was not blocked, giving the speaker control of the victim and a file created on its desktop as proof. The main takeaway is that defenders should validate their controls with offensive techniques, rather than treating one product result as a verdict on which product is best. The speaker said findings were reported to the vendors involved.

talks.title: Attacking Modern Environments Series Attack Vectors on Terraform Environments Inbox by Mazin A.
talks.teaser: Shows how Terraform state files, Enterprise instances and public providers can give attackers a path into cloud accounts.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Terraform, HashiCorp's infrastructure-as-code tool, can become a route into cloud accounts. The speaker walks through how plan and apply work and why the state file is valuable: it keeps copies of secrets such as database credentials and access keys, so read access to a remote state bucket can expose much of what an organisation deploys. Self-hosted Terraform Enterprise instances hold the same data and usually run with broad cloud permissions, and their API can return the full state to a user with the right access.

The middle section covers code execution through pull requests. A developer token that can push feature branches to a repository linked to Terraform can introduce a malicious external data source, which runs during plan and gives a shell on the server. The speaker notes that a fix proposed in 2018 was rejected and that other tools built on plan workflows face the same exposure. The main demonstration is an evil provider: a backdoored provider published to the public registry was approved and executed inside Terraform Cloud, and none of the uploaded samples were flagged by VirusTotal. The speaker stopped at proof of execution, and HashiCorp's security team contacted him within hours.

The closing recommendations cover restricting bucket policies on state storage, keeping Terraform instances in isolated private networks, reviewing them regularly because they make strong persistence points, limiting write access to repositories, treating state files as sensitive, and adding CI checks that flag unexpected providers.

talks.title: Keeping Up With Modern Automotive Exploitation by Kamel Ghali
talks.teaser: Walks through recent automotive hacks, from Bluetooth and Wi-Fi entry points to key fob and infotainment compromises.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys recent public attacks on modern vehicles for listeners new to automotive security. It explains why car hacks carry physical safety stakes, and outlines the UN regulation and ISO/SAE 21434 standard that push manufacturers toward formal cyber testing. The multi-tier supplier chain is presented as a reason adoption across the industry is slow.

Three case studies follow. A 2020 Lexus study showed remote code execution through a Bluetooth stack flaw in the infotainment unit, which led to a Wi-Fi backdoor, a reflashed secondary controller and disabled CAN filters. A 2020 Tesla Model X study abused unsigned Bluetooth firmware updates on the key fob, letting a cloned fob be paired to the body control module so the car could be driven away. A 2021 Tesla study chained a ConnMan DNS flaw, reached through a spoofed service network, with an information leak to bypass DEP and ASLR and gain control of the infotainment system.

The shared lesson is that short-range wireless interfaces become entry points when firmware signing and layer separation are missing. The speaker urges signed updates, network segmentation and sandboxing, plus product vulnerability management that maps new advisories onto every component. He closes by encouraging engineers to consider automotive security as a specialty.

talks.title: Skrull Like A King From File Unlink to Persistence by: Sheng-Hao Ma
talks.teaser: Shows how malware can run fileless and evade antivirus scans and automatic sample submission, using Windows process tricks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem defenders face: antivirus products scan new processes in real time and can automatically send suspicious samples to vendors, where researchers then study them. The speaker frames the attacker's side as three problems: getting code into a trusted-looking process without triggering detection, keeping the injection itself from being scanned, and stopping an analyst from studying a sample that reaches a vendor.

The first technique creates a process from a file that is later overwritten with harmless data, so the kernel's process-creation notification only sees a clean file. A second method marks a temporary file as delete-pending, so no scanner can open it, then creates a process from it and removes the file, leaving a process with no name or path. The speaker demonstrated this with Mimikatz, which Defender blocked when run directly but ran when launched this way. A third method uses NTFS streams to move a running executable's data elsewhere, which lets the file be deleted and makes the process appear to carry a Microsoft signature. The speaker noted the process-creation trick was first presented in 2017 and that Windows Defender could detect it by 2021.

These ideas are combined into a launcher that fingerprints the victim, rebuilds itself from that data, decrypts the payload only in memory, and destroys itself if it is sent to a vendor, so researchers cannot reproduce it. The main takeaway for defenders is that scanning files on disk is not enough; running processes need to be analysed too.

The presentation opens on the global cybersecurity talent crunch, citing millions of unfilled roles, rising compensation, and the puzzle of why many candidates still struggle to land jobs. The speaker frames a security career as an adventure game with early, mid, and end stages.

For newcomers, the early game covers choosing an entry role without overthinking, the expectation that teams need useful people from day one, and a trio of education, hands-on experience, and certifications. Advice includes home labs, CTFs, bug bounties, fundamentals in networking, scripting, and Linux, focused specialization over being average everywhere, consulting for exposure to mature practices, mentor outreach, and certification strategy that favors major credentials and real learning over collecting papers.

Mid-game guidance stresses technical depth plus functional knowledge such as governance, industry context, and translating risk into business terms, alongside communication, reporting, and patience. End-game tips cover modeling successful leaders, improving craft over overtime, networking without burning bridges, community contribution, imposter syndrome, and sustaining passion through a long marathon.

talks.title: Bug Bounty 101
talks.teaser: Walks newcomers through common web bug classes, Burp Suite basics and tips for writing clear bug bounty reports.

This beginner session introduces bug bounty hunting by first explaining HTTP basics: requests, methods, hosts and cookies. It then shows Burp Suite as an intercepting proxy for viewing and modifying traffic, including routing a SQLMap run through it so its requests can be inspected.

The middle of the talk works through bug classes by application feature, with live demonstrations on a deliberately vulnerable test application. These include account registration without rate limiting, login brute forcing, and EXIF GPS metadata surviving an image upload. Password reset issues are covered too: unlimited reset emails, token reuse, token leakage to third parties through the referrer header, and sessions that stay valid after a password change. The speaker also covers broken link hijacking via unclaimed social media handles, HTML injection in notification emails, and horizontal and vertical access control flaws, shown with separate test accounts.

The closing section offers reporting advice. Read the program brief first, include full HTTP requests with dynamic values marked, and write short, step-by-step proof of concept instructions. Add screenshots, use video only when a bug is hard to reproduce, and always explain the security impact so triagers can judge the issue.

talks.title: Using Wordpress comments section as a CC for fun by Juan Karlo Licudineaccidentalrebel
talks.teaser: Explores how moderated WordPress comment preview links enable covert two-way bot command traffic on third-party blogs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames command-and-control as the channel malware uses to issue orders and collect stolen data, then describes building a remote access tool that initially relied on a dedicated server. Prior work on evasive C2 over public platforms motivates hunting for another everyday service, and WordPress is chosen because anonymous comments need only a name and email.

The first design hides operator commands inside spam comments on unmoderated blogs, with bots polling the thread and replying the same way. Auto-moderation breaks visibility, so the approach pivots to WordPress preview URLs for comments held in the queue. Because previews expire in about ten minutes, bots must reconstruct the same link the operator sees. Open-source review shows URLs combine a post permalink, an unapproved comment index, and an MD5 moderation hash tied to comment time plus site secrets. Bots brute-force the operator’s index, then post in the same minute-level window so their hash matches without reading wp-config.php. A scheduled ten-minute cadence, live proof-of-concept, and duplicate-comment acknowledgments round out bidirectional exfiltration.

Practitioners should treat this as practical abuse of a legitimate moderation feature: public pages stay clean while queues fill with noise. Defenders may spot floods of moderated spam; anti-spam plugins and future preview changes limit viability. The speaker notes pooling many small blogs to spread load and points to a public project for full mechanics.

talks.title: The Curious case of knowing the unknown by Vandana Verma Sehgal
talks.teaser: Surveys open-source supply chain blind spots and shows how stale IDE extensions can leak developer files before attackers find them.
talks.summary:
Home robots and connected devices illustrate how little owners may know about where software updates and stored data actually live. The talk pivots to application delivery: containers, serverless, bare metal, and the reality that most shipped code is open source, with a large share of reported flaws sitting in indirect dependencies rather than code teams wrote themselves. Security programs that lean on traditional app scanning alone miss the majority of what runs in production.

The middle of the session strings together well-known supply chain failures and research—compiler trust chains, maintainer-focused npm attacks, widely downloaded packages with slow or absent fixes, weak registry credentials, IDE repository compromise, maintainer removals that broke installs, and spikes of malicious packages on public registries. A browser demo uses an outdated Visual Studio Code markdown extension: visiting a hostile page triggers exfiltration of files from the developer home directory, including material an attacker could abuse for further access.

The closing emphasis is operational visibility before outsiders exploit the same gaps: know what is installed in dev and build environments, scan dependencies and images continuously, track transitive risk, and use software bills of materials to prioritize fixes. Security and development need shared ownership when severity shifts after unrelated changes, so the ecosystem is understood end to end.

talks.title: Phishing & Education Applying security principles during the pandemic by IJ Puzon
talks.teaser: Walks through a phishing investigation from 2020 in the Philippines and how a church-run school moved to remote learning.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a phishing case from August 2020 that the speaker helped a victim investigate in the Philippines. A phishing email posing as a local bank reached the victim early on a Friday morning, and its link led to a web server with directory listing and an exposed admin panel, which suggested a compromised host. Header analysis done in a plain text editor, read from the bottom up, showed the message passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks, so the receiving mail service treated it as legitimate. Posts and login records from the accused account were then lined up against the timeline.

The middle section looks at deception beyond email. Examples include a fake Facebook security checkpoint hosted on a Google Sites page, a giveaway quiz that redirected to an unrelated site, and a login page that accepted any username and password. A minor's compromised account spread one such link to a group. The speaker also showed a 2021 document exploit as a proof of concept that launched the calculator, and argued that government and school domains should be easy to verify so people can tell real contacts from look-alikes.

The second half describes how a church-run school moved to remote learning during the pandemic. The team chose Office 365 over G Suite because parents and teachers already knew it, it had no class time limit, and Teams used less data. They enabled multi-factor authentication and tracked their security compliance score. Takeaways include understanding business processes, building security in from the start, knowing your assets, and admitting mistakes.

talks.title: Zero Trust in the era of cloud by: Vandana Verma Sehgal aka InfosecVandana
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Zero Trust in the era of cloud by: Vandana Verma Sehgal aka InfosecVandana.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Vandana Verma Sehgal explores the shift from legacy boundary-based security models to Zero Trust architectures, specifically within the context of cloud adoption and distributed remote work. She explains that traditional network security operated under the assumption that internal users and traffic were inherently trustworthy. However, the rise of insider threats, credential theft, advanced persistent threats (APTs), and perimeter-less cloud deployments invalidates perimeter defenses. The presentation highlights that Zero Trust is not a single product or bolt-on tool, but a fundamental security strategy that flips the old mantra of "trust, but verify" into "never trust, always verify."

### Key Topics
- **Deficiencies of Traditional Perimeters:** Relying on physical office walls, firewalls, and broad network zones fails when remote work expands and malicious actors obtain legitimate administrative credentials or exploit insider access.
- **Cost and Frequency of Breaches:** Citing statistics from Cyber Security Ventures and Ponemon/IBM, the talk notes rising cybersecurity costs ($6 trillion by 2021) and breach costs ($3.62 million average), highlighting that roughly 80% of data breaches involve privileged access abuse.
- **Core Tenets of Zero Trust:** The model assumes environments are hostile, emphasizing the continuous verification of users and devices, strict access governance, and establishing micro-perimeters.
- **Architectural Planes and Protect Surfaces:** Zero Trust differentiates between the control plane (management and configuration) and the data plane. It focuses on identifying and securing a specific "protect surface" consisting of critical data, applications, and services.
- **Modern Identity and Access Management (IAM):** Identity acts as the new perimeter. Organizations must move beyond static Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to context-aware, adaptive access controls, Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), and Just-In-Time (JIT) least-privilege models.

### Technical Details
- **Network Segmentation & Gateways:** Enterprises should create micro-perimeters using segmentation gateways (such as Next-Generation Firewalls) to gain granular application-layer visibility and block lateral movement or data exfiltration.
- **Traffic Encryption & Telemetry:** All network traffic must be encrypted regardless of origin. Continuous zone-wise logging and monitoring are required to preserve audit trails for post-incident analysis.
- **Data Categorization:** Security teams must classify information (e.g., confidential, internal, restricted, or public) to avoid wasting defensive resources on non-critical data while ensuring sensitive data (such as PII or payment card data) is strictly governed.
- **Identity Best Practices:** Avoid using root or master cloud accounts for everyday development; instead, use delegated administrator roles and separate permissions across production environments. To bridge legacy software into modern authentication flows (such as SAML, OAuth, or OIDC), organizations can place reverse proxies or web seals in front of legacy systems.
- **Cloud Shared Responsibility & Contracts:** Addressing an audience question regarding SOC 2 reports and cloud contracts, Sehgal stresses that while third-party audits must sometimes be relied upon when providers forbid direct penetration testing, organizations remain accountable for securing their own assets, configurations, and cloud storage (such as AWS S3 buckets).

### Takeaways
Zero Trust implementation requires incremental adoption across the entire organization rather than isolated deployments. Security teams should prioritize identifying sensitive data, mapping data flows, establishing micro-perimeters, enforcing least privilege, and automating detection and response workflows.

talks.title: Pursuing Evasive Custom Command & Control C3 by: Mark Ian Secretario / Renzon Cruz
talks.teaser: Practitioners see how attackers abuse SaaS for C2, how C3 extends red-team tooling, and which logs expose those channels.
talks.summary:
The presenters frame command and control as a late kill-chain stage that many security teams under-prioritize compared with perimeter delivery. They describe how adversaries hide in ordinary enterprise traffic by routing implants through widely trusted web and cloud services—Slack, Twitter, Gmail, Office 365, OneDrive, Dropbox, and similar channels—often keeping callbacks low, slow, and timed like normal user activity.

After a primer on traditional beaconing and MITRE ATT&CK mappings, they walk through concrete abuse cases such as OneDrive-backed Empire activity, Kalido-style Microsoft Graph paths, and prior APT use of social and storage APIs. The core demonstration introduces F-Secure and MWR Labs C3 as a modular external C2 gateway that plugs into frameworks like Covenant and Cobalt Strike, with live relays over Slack, Dropbox, UNC shares, Google Drive, and GitHub. Demos run across home, AWS, and Azure lab stacks built from open detection-lab style environments with Splunk, ELK, Sysmon, Zeek, and process-chain visibility.

The defensive half turns those executions into hunt and detection guidance: PowerShell module and transcript logging, encoded command lines, Sysmon network and DNS events, beacon intervals with jitter, JA3 TLS fingerprints, unsigned binaries calling cloud APIs, ETW considerations, and Splunk queries tied to technique IDs. They recommend inventorying available telemetry, mapping controls to ATT&CK, and pairing open tools such as RITA, JA3 lookups, and the C2 Matrix with IAM hardening, Office 365 audit logs, and network restrictions on unsanctioned cloud storage where policy allows.

Rod presents Attack Range, a tool that builds test environments for detection engineering and adversary simulation. He covers two deployment paths: a local version using Vagrant and VirtualBox on a laptop, and a cloud version on AWS built with Terraform and Ansible. A typical lab can include a Windows domain controller, a Windows client, a Linux host, a Splunk server and a Kali machine, with Sysmon and the Splunk Universal Forwarder sending logs to Splunk. Rod recommends treating cloud labs as disposable, destroying them after each test to limit cost and exposure.

The demonstrations ran Atomic Red Team and Caldera against the Windows host, then searched the resulting events in Splunk. Rod also showed how a detection from the ESCU content library ties back to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, such as OS credential dumping. A Caldera discovery profile reported which steps succeeded, such as listing local and active users, while antivirus discovery did not. A cloud-only variant followed, using the Leonidas simulation framework to generate AWS activity that appeared in CloudTrail logs.

The main takeaway is that adversary simulation measures how detection and response behave, ideally against a golden image that matches a real corporate build. It does not replace penetration tests or red team work, cannot stop zero-day exploits, and cannot replicate every technique. Rod warned that once a technique or detection is public, adversaries may adapt, and that frameworks should not be left running inside a live perimeter.

talks.title: Car Hacking Village (RC14 Recovery Mode)
talks.teaser: Surveys Car Hacking Village PH at ROOTCON, community labs, starter CAN gear, and how mechanics literacy supports automotive security work.
talks.summary:
The recording begins as an orientation to Car Hacking Village PH, tied to ROOTCON’s recovery-mode program and inspired by the main DEF CON village. Organizers recap launches from ROOTCON 13 onward, virtual appearances, and hands-on history with instrument clusters, Craig Smith–style virtual clusters, ECU simulators, UDS interaction, and an anomaly-detection proof of concept from collaborators in India. They explain goals of building a local community, finding safety-relevant weaknesses, and assembling a more complete test bench—including Mazda and BMW ECU kits and a future physical car donors might supply—while stressing research without destroying hardware.

Most of the middle is interactive Q&A aimed at newcomers: inexpensive eBay clusters and ECU kits, sensible first platforms, CAN bus versus infotainment and broader IoT surfaces, OBD2 and security-gateway bypass concepts, rolling-code key attacks, bug bashes and telematics, electric-vehicle battery-management risks, and how experiments can affect airbags, lighting, or ECU state. Presenters repeatedly steer people toward The Car Hacker’s Handbook, NanoCAN, CAN utilities, fuzzing references, and other curated vehicle-security resources.

The latter portion turns hands-on but non-exploit: one speaker teaches baseline engine diagnostics with OBD2 scanners, multimeters, and common sensor failures, using misfire and fuel-trim examples so attendees can relate bus-visible behavior to real symptoms. Another starts a segment on electronic fuel injection, ECU inputs, and dashboard fault indications as groundwork for lawful tuning and tinkering, explicitly bridging wrench skills with the village’s hacking track for the year.

talks.title: Hacking 101 Training (RC14 Recovery Mode Edition)
talks.teaser: Training covers hacking fundamentals, career and lab essentials, bug bounties, penetration tools, and a repeatable methodology.
talks.summary:
The opening segment frames hacking as altering systems beyond their intended purpose, walks through hacker archetypes, and argues that moving from novice to capable practitioner requires sustained study across software, operating systems, and networking. It lays out essentials such as community engagement, reference material, a home lab, capture-the-flag practice, documentation, conferences, bug bounty platforms, certifications, personal security hygiene, and familiar tools ranging from browser inspectors to Burp Suite, Metasploit, and Wireshark. The presenter also shares a personal path from web development through static application security testing into penetration testing and application security engineering, plus brief notes on Philippine security entrepreneurs.

The second segment shifts to penetration testing: how it differs from vulnerability assessment, why proof-of-concept exploitation matters in reports, and how organizations often underestimate risk. It illustrates vulnerability classes with examples such as remote code execution, resource-exhaustion denial of service after reversing a downloadable applet, and ties findings to bug bounty categories like server-side template injection and local file inclusion. A tool survey covers nmap, netcat, bind and reverse shells, directory brute forcing, sqlmap, Hydra, OpenVAS, Burp Suite, Responder, Metasploit, Wireshark, hashcat, and Mimikatz.

The close presents a repeatable methodology—information gathering, vulnerability identification, exploitation, post-exploitation, and reporting—and walks through a Drupal-oriented lab chain from port scanning to remote code execution, privilege escalation to root, and data exfiltration. A certification roadmap and Q&A stress that hands-on experience outweighs credentials alone while still valuing structured learning paths such as eJPT, CEH, and OSCP.

talks.title: Hackers Don't Wear Black Hoodies, They Wear Capes by: Chloé Messdaghi
talks.teaser: Connects disclosure fear, CFAA case studies, and media stereotypes to a five-step plan for shifting laws and public trust.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames hacker rights as protection for people who report flaws, face prosecution, or advocate for clearer rules. It surveys why many researchers stay silent: pre-breach warnings ignored at major companies, surveys showing most do not report, and distrust when vulnerability disclosure programs are missing or unclear.

Case studies anchor the argument. A drone vendor’s in-house bounty allegedly offered payment without legal safe harbor and pursued CFAA claims despite in-scope work. Hired penetration testers waited for police after an alarm at a courthouse and still spent a night in jail. The speaker contrasts ethical hackers who stay in scope with attackers who exploit, then uses a cognitive-science metaphor about learned stereotypes to explain why hoodies and criminal labels in media fuel fear and block bilateral trust with organizations.

The closing maps outdated U.S. law—CFAA origins, Aaron Swartz, failed Aaron’s Law, DMCA’s research limits—and highlights Van Buren v. United States as terms-of-service overreach. A three-part public cycle ties press language, corporate disclosure programs, and legislation. Five participation steps include petitions, hackingisnotacrime.org, correcting media wording, adopting VDPs, lobbying representatives, and backing groups such as EFF and disclose.io.

talks.teaser: A walkthrough of repurposing a scrapyard head unit and bench-wiring ECUs into a portable automotive hacking lab.
talks.summary:
The presenter traces a path from compromising an in-vehicle infotainment head unit on a Citroën DS5 to building a bench-mounted Peugeot 208 lab that behaves like a real car without wheels. Early work started with boredom and nmap while tethered to the dashboard unit, uncovering telnet, exposed personal data stores, and weaknesses reachable over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth PAN, followed by disclosure friction with the manufacturer and salvage-yard sourcing of a standalone head unit awakened by replayed CAN traffic.

Funding from a later coordinated vehicle security assessment supported expanding the rig: coded modules, diagnostic chaos, crank and cam signal simulation with ArguStim, lambda and ABS wheel-speed fakery, and four separate CAN networks with extra OBD-II taps for hands-on demos. Low-cost NanoCAN and TinyCAN adapters illustrate listening, injection, and playful dash effects such as disco mode.

Practitioners hear candid lessons about bricking gear on the OBD port, why full engine harnesses dwarf kit-car wiring, and how to teach conference audiences vehicle attacks without shipping an entire automobile overseas.

talks.title: ReconPal Leveraging NLP for Infosec by: Nishant Sharma & Jeswin Mathai
talks.teaser: Shows a Telegram bot that turns plain-English requests into Shodan searches, nmap scans and attacks via GPT-3.
talks.summary:
The talk presents ReconPal, a Telegram bot that takes plain-English requests from a penetration tester and works out which reconnaissance or attack tool to run. The speakers explain the pipeline: the bot passes the text to the OpenAI API, which returns the module, tool and operation to use. The controller then routes the job to a finder module that queries Shodan, a scanner module running nmap, or an attacker module running tools such as Hydra. Each part runs in its own Docker container, and the containers communicate over websockets.

The demo first searched Shodan for exposed cameras, Docker TCP sockets, Portainer instances and Memcached servers, using natural-language queries. Because the speakers lacked permission to touch public hosts, the scanning and attack steps ran against a deliberately vulnerable machine inside a private AWS VPC. There, nmap found a vulnerable vsftpd version on port 21, dirb and Nikto enumerated the web application, and SQLMap found no injectable parameters. A Memcached check confirmed the server could be abused for amplified DDoS, and a Hydra dictionary attack recovered a weak password.

The speakers noted practical barriers: the OpenAI API was in beta with a long waitlist, and Shodan API access is paid. The planned version 2 adds audio input, lets the model build commands from tool documentation, summarises output and offers interactive attacker sessions. Version 3 would test other language models to reduce cost.

talks.teaser: Shows how enriching hunting and investigative feeds turns raw security telemetry into operational intelligence for faster decisions.
talks.summary:
The session frames operational intelligence around the gap between raw telemetry and what analysts need during hunts and investigations. Early material stresses that security teams struggle to locate and trust the right data across disparate sources, and that enrichment is what makes entries usable by adding context such as geographic detail, producer metadata, and relationships that plain logs lack.

The middle walks through building enrichment into daily workflows: combining multiple source types, normalizing entries, and using pipelines or platforms (including elastic-style search stacks) to attach indicators, login and network patterns, and cross-border or multi-location connection examples where the captions remain intelligible. The speaker points to bi-directional or recurring checks, automated collection, and optional machine-learning assistance so enrichment scales beyond manual typing.

The close ties enrichment to concrete outcomes: mapping measurements on network data, tightening alert and notification flows, and shrinking the time from event to judgment. The intended takeaway is that mature enrichment architecture—fed by open approaches to projects and integrations—gives investigators richer, more efficient information without treating every field as an isolated datapoint.

talks.title: Farewell WAF Exploiting SQL Injection from Mutation to Polymorphism
talks.teaser: Shows how SQL injection payloads can be mutated and reshaped to slip past web application firewalls.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how SQL injection payloads can get past web application firewalls. It starts from the point where a filter inspects a request and blocks a known malicious pattern, then shows how changing the form of a statement, rather than its meaning, can let an injection through the filter while the database still executes it.

The middle section contrasts two families of rewriting. Mutation makes small changes to pieces of a statement, while the polymorphic approach transforms the structure so the query keeps its behaviour under a different surface. The speaker describes variants that replace only a single fragment and others that replace a wider part of the statement, including its operators, and explains how those transformations are applied in order.

Near the end, the talk turns to protections and frames them as a counterpart to the techniques shown earlier. The practical takeaway is that filters built on fixed patterns are fragile against rewritten payloads, so defenders should not rely on signature-style matching alone and should handle untrusted input correctly inside the application.

talks.title: Navigating the Shift from Opportunistic to Targeted Ransomware Attacks
talks.teaser: Traces how ransomware gangs moved from mass infections to hand-picked victims, and what that shift means for defenders.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how ransomware has moved away from opportunistic mass infection toward deliberately chosen victims. It starts with the ransomware-as-a-service model, in which developers rent their malware to affiliates who carry out the intrusions. The speaker describes how affiliates working at volume were paid roughly $3,000 per infection, which pushed operators to spread widely and made handling many victims through chat support slow and costly.

The middle of the talk covers the targeted approach. Instead of spreading broadly, attackers research a single organisation, such as a large corporation or a city government, and negotiate one-on-one with a demand that can reach millions of dollars. The speaker explains the operational steps that come with this, including stopping running processes and services so files can be encrypted, and disrupting existing backups. Organisations that hold sensitive data, and providers of services or infrastructure, are named as the likely targets.

The closing part draws practical lessons for defenders. The speaker notes that attackers often find public information about a company's technology during their research, and stresses having the ability to recover after an infection. Known indicators of compromise are pointed out as signs to watch for, and the decision to pay is framed as a business judgment that depends on how long operations would be disrupted.

talks.title: The Role of Hackers in Securing the Country's Cyberspace
talks.teaser: Urges skilled hackers to use their talents to defend the Philippines' cyberspace as warfare moves online.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a reflection on how warfare has changed over time, from sticks, stones, spears and swords to the aircraft and machines of the world wars, and on to weapons of mass destruction and guided weapons. The speaker argues that conflict now increasingly takes place through digital means, and that cyber attacks can reach power supplies, communication networks and other critical infrastructure.

Against that background, the speaker describes national efforts in the Philippines. It refers to a yearly national observance of cybersecurity in September set by the president, and to the organization of a Cyber Command in response to a national cybersecurity call. The speaker notes that this capability is still being built.

The closing part is an appeal to hackers and technically skilled people to put their abilities at the service of the nation and to join the wider effort toward a secure Philippine cyberspace. The speaker draws on a Bible passage about using one's talents and ability, and frames the work as a shared responsibility rather than a task for a few specialists.

talks.title: Data Privacy and Security; Accountability and Assurance in the Digital Age by: Raymund Liboro
talks.teaser: Shows accountability and assurance where privacy law meets security practice, tied to national digital identity rollout and risk mapping.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from the perspective of a national privacy regulator in a country pushing rapid digitization. Personal data has become a primary economic asset and cross-border data flows have exploded, while citizens expect both convenience from cloud and government services and protection from misuse ranging from discrimination to loss of autonomy. The Philippines’ data privacy framework is positioned alongside a growing community of global privacy jurisdictions.

The middle of the talk separates information security from data privacy in plain operational terms: security addresses confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data, whereas privacy addresses how incidents affect people through collection, use, storage, and sharing. Accountability and assurance extend beyond technical controls to governance and insider risk, with breach statistics cited to argue that a large share of harm still comes from authorized insiders and preventable process failures, not only external attackers.

The close ties these ideas to government digital transformation, especially a rolling national ID program. Leadership is portrayed as trying to harmonize privacy and security rather than treat them as opposites when laws, policies, and skilled reviewers exist. The regulator describes participating in rulemaking, pushing mandatory disclosure for malicious activity in the ID system, and launching a voluntary assessment initiative—recruiting roughly thirty conference attendees—to map risks and strengthen institutions before wider deployment.

talks.title: How to not Fail at Hardware by: Craig Smith
talks.teaser: Covers scoping, black-box testing and vendor disclosure lessons drawn from hardware work on vehicle devices.
talks.summary:
Craig Smith, who leads research for a transportation security team, opens with a problem many testers face: taking on hardware work they have little experience with. He argues that the hesitation is often misplaced, because most core security questions carry over from software engagements, and that success is decided largely during scoping. He recommends narrowing a hardware project to its security-relevant parts, guided by a threat model, instead of trying to cover every component.

He then draws on earlier vehicle research. In one case, the manufacturer's legal team sent cease-and-desist letters after findings were reported, a reaction he contrasts with how security researchers usually respond. In a black-box exercise on a device with no documentation, he traced its circuit board, wiring and processor, and tested how its update package was handled. A modified update was applied and changed the device's start screen. He explains that vehicle designs often take about five years to reach the road, and that support can run more than a decade, so older weaknesses persist.

The closing advice centres on the vendor relationship. Issues raised late, after a product is set, are costly for manufacturers and often go unfixed, so testers should raise them early with the manufacturer and its suppliers. Practitioners should agree on scope with clients, set realistic timelines, and push for security requirements to enter the hardware development lifecycle at the design stage.
