talks.title: Apple Health by: Vladimir Katalov
talks.teaser: Shows how forensic examiners extract Apple Health data from iPhones, iCloud and backups, and where the protections fall short.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at what health data an iPhone's Health app keeps and how it can be obtained. The speaker explains that the data comes from the phone's own sensors, paired wearables and third-party fitness apps, and that it is stored across several SQLite databases and exported files rather than in one readable format. The analysis is framed around recovering that data for investigations.

The middle of the talk covers the acquisition routes. The in-app export produces a zip archive with XML files. An encrypted iTunes backup is another option. A full file system extraction with forensic software gives more data, but on the versions discussed it required a jailbreak, and the speaker mentions a vendor claim of acquisition without one. When Health sync is enabled, data also reaches iCloud, where it is encrypted with keys stored apart from the data. The main obstacle to cloud access is two-factor authentication. The speaker describes token-based access from trusted devices as a way around it in some cases, and notes that a cloud records request can take about a week.

The closing point is that health data is spread across the device, backups and the cloud, so the protections on the Apple account, trusted devices and backup encryption largely decide how much of it can be recovered.

talks.title: Panel Discussion: Philippine National ID System
talks.teaser: A panel weighs identity federation, citizen privacy risks, and practical security gaps in the Philippine national ID rollout.
talks.summary:
The panel opens on why the Philippines pursued a unified national ID: government agencies historically each held separate identifiers, while the deeper aim is one consistent way to prove who someone is and eventually support federated access to digital services, comparable in spirit to OpenID-style identity sharing.

Panelists and audience members contrast convenience—seamless transactions and doing business—with privacy and abuse risks if biographic or biometric data is misused or breached. They note much demographic data already exists in siloed systems, yet centralizing attributes can still widen impact when things go wrong. Discussion turns to securing the platform through authentication models, critical security controls, and the harder work of operations and budget priorities, alongside fears about weak physical issuance, counterfeits, and optional features such as mobile-linked data.

The conversation closes on breach realism, negligence versus preparedness, auditing federated logins, limiting who may delegate authentication, and whether structured researcher disclosure or bug bounty style programs should complement agency websites. Practitioners hear a call to help shape a least-bad rollout with responsible security review rather than treating the ID as a solved problem.

talks.title: pi$$ing off an APT by: Ed Williams
talks.teaser: Explains how defenders can frustrate an APT by hardening basics and targeting attacker behaviour over easy indicators.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how organisations can make life harder for advanced persistent threat groups. The speaker argues that red team exercises and simulations are useful, but that resilience also depends on detection and response, and that teams should mature across both process and technology rather than relying on tools alone. A "triangle of pain" model is used to show the trade-off: easily changed indicators such as IP addresses and DNS records are quick for attackers to replace, while changes to their tactics, techniques and procedures cost them far more.

The middle of the talk covers the basics. The speaker describes how attackers map an environment through public DNS and MX records and cloud-hosted services, and how phishing and exposed internet-facing software can provide initial access. Defensive basics highlighted include segregating networks, avoiding shared privileged passwords, and patching consistently. Password guidance covers minimum length, checking choices against dictionaries of common or breached passwords, and questioning forced periodic expiry. SMS as a second factor is criticised as weak. The speaker also stresses logging enough activity to spot attacker behaviour, since gaps in logging let intruders move unseen.

The closing part returns to the idea that no single fix stops an APT. The practical takeaway is that the cheapest gains come from getting fundamentals right, while detection and response capability is built to catch behaviour that gets past them.

talks.title: Bug Bounty Hunting on Steroids by: Anshuman Bhartiya
talks.teaser: Shows how chained, containerized recon workers can automate scanning and reporting for bug bounty hunters.
talks.summary:
Bug bounty work is often slowed by many open-source tools that repeat the same job, and the talk argues for a more unified way to run them. It walks through a containerized framework in which each tool runs as a worker, so dependencies are packaged and the environment can be reproduced. Steps are defined in a pipeline where the output of one stage becomes the input of the next.

A live demo starts a chain of scanning steps against a target. The early stages scan ports, and their output feeds later tools that identify services. The workflow then reports its findings, including a password-related result, with little manual effort once the steps were defined. The speaker notes that adding a new step means extending the workflow definition rather than rewriting the process.

The speaker describes building the project over roughly two years, starting from a minimal version and setting aside the more complicated pieces to ship an MVP. The closing advice is to keep the framework simple and extensible so that others can contribute to it.

talks.title: Not So Crab Mentality: A True RasS Story by: Christopher Elisan
talks.teaser: Researchers follow a Russian RaaS recruit-from-forum model through affiliate panels, metamorphic persistence, and victim payment flows.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames ransomware as a service as a partnership economy on Russian-language underground forums, where skilled authors supply malware and affiliates contribute bulletproof hosting, access, or spam without building the payload themselves. A recurring forum persona keeps reposting partnership ads for ransomware branded as Dan Crab or Gap Crab, offering revenue splits and emphasizing that operators need little technical skill while the author retains infrastructure-heavy work.

Through a training narrative, the speakers walk from those ads into an operator web panel that tracks infections worldwide, payment status, and success rates used to refine the malware. Technical attention centers on Gap Crab’s use of the RunOnce registry key for persistence and metamorphism: each reboot removes one on-disk copy while spawning a renamed variant, which complicates cleanup after restart. The talk also covers Tor-based payment pages, escalating ransoms, multilingual support, free trial decryption, and the gap between receiving a decryptor and removing residual malware.

Practitioners are pointed toward communal decryption resources such as No More Ransom, warned that quiet self-payment is common among corporate travelers, and reminded to isolate machines and avoid copying recovered files onto systems that may still harbor the strain. The arc closes with the cautionary outcome that casual affiliation with such services carries serious legal risk.

talks.title: Exploiting ActionScript3 Interpreter by: Boris Larin
talks.teaser: Shows how an ActionScript3 interpreter's exception handling can be abused to gain control over memory.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the basics of ActionScript3, the language that runs inside a virtual machine in Flash, and how its instructions are interpreted. The speaker describes the interpreter's structure and notes that some existing analysis tools do not support Flash files, which makes the engine harder to study.

The core of the talk is a bug in how the interpreter handles exceptions. The speaker shows that a function dealing with an exception can be entered a second time while the session state is already set, so the engine takes an unexpected path. Using a jump instruction that triggers an exception, the speaker walks through how the interpreter routes control through its exception structures, and how that flow can be pushed into a state where internal values and memory can be influenced.

Toward the end, the speaker explains how a debug build helped follow the interpreter's behaviour during exploitation, and how a later version addressed the issue. A practitioner should take away that logic inside a script engine, such as exception handling and re-entry into handlers, can be as exploitable as a classic memory bug, and that fixes need to check whether a handler can be called again while it is still running.

talks.title: Car Infotainment Hacking Methodology and Attack Surface Scenarios by: Jay Turla
talks.teaser: Maps infotainment attack surfaces in cars, from Bluetooth and USB to Wi-Fi and firmware updates, through real-world scenarios.
talks.summary:
The talk maps the attack surface of car infotainment consoles, the head units that handle media, navigation and phone connectivity. The speaker, an application security engineer, presents a methodology of listing exposed interfaces first and then probing each one. Bluetooth comes first, with examples of jamming the link, abusing default pairing PINs, and memory corruption that can crash the device and sometimes drop it into a desktop environment.

Other interfaces follow. USB ports and SD cards are shown as routes to running code, including a demo where a USB device made the console execute a script. Over Wi-Fi, the speaker scans a head unit with nmap and finds telnet, FTP and SSH services that accept connections without authentication or with default credentials. Firmware updates are another weak point when signature validation is missing. Cellular links and a companion mobile app are also discussed, where intercepted requests showed remote car functions with no authentication.

The talk closes with disclosure. Several findings were reported to manufacturers, and the speaker points to vendor bug bounty channels for submitting issues. The takeaway for practitioners is to inventory every interface on a vehicle head unit, check whether services require authentication, and verify that firmware updates are signed.

talks.title: Finding Your Way to Domain Admin Access and Even So, the Game Isn't Over Yet by: Keith Lee
talks.teaser: Follows an attacker's path from one compromised host to domain admin through credential harvesting and lateral movement.
talks.summary:
The talk follows an attacker's route from a first foothold on a Windows network to domain admin rights. It starts from the problem that a single compromised machine often gives limited access, so the focus moves to harvesting credentials stored on that host and reusing them elsewhere. Shared local administrator passwords are presented as a way access can spread across many machines once one is recovered.

The middle section covers where credentials and misconfigurations tend to appear. Group Policy Preferences are described as keeping passwords in a default folder that any domain user can reach. The talk also looks at a Kerberos-related weakness, impersonation and delegation tokens, and an application whitelisting setup that can be bypassed with scripts. Process listings on each machine help identify which programs and services are worth targeting, and a demo walks through moving between hosts in a small environment.

The closing part looks at what happens after privileged access is obtained and how an attacker can keep a foothold in place. The advice for defenders centres on not reusing the same password across systems and removing credentials left in shared locations, and on treating each compromised host as one step rather than the end of the intrusion.

talks.title: Hacking Robots Before Skynet by: Lucas Apa
talks.teaser: Networked robots broadcast discoverable services, and the session traces research into restarting processes to seize operational control.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames commercial and research robots as always-on networked hosts that advertise services instead of staying invisible on corporate LANs. That visibility becomes the starting point for offensive security work aimed at platforms deployed in malls, workplaces, and similar environments where people treat machines as appliances rather than computers.

Much of the middle follows hands-on research against a rover-style robot stack. The speaker describes probing services, hitting refused connections, and digging into how the control software runs on the backing computer. A central thread is forcing a restart so a fresh instance comes up in a state that weakens filtering, then using elevated command paths to read status and influence motion or shutdown behavior. Demonstrations tie those steps to real operator panels and live responses from the device.

For defenders and testers, the implied lesson is to inventory robot VLANs, monitor their service banners, and harden process isolation on embedded controllers. Attackers gain leverage when the same management interface trusted for fleet updates can be reached after a manipulated restart. The Skynet framing underscores urgency: these systems are already online before any hypothetical future autonomy crisis.

talks.title: Demystifying the Ransomware and IoT Threat by: Christopher Elisan
talks.teaser: Narrative walkthroughs show how invoice lures, SVG tricks, and weak IoT credentials feed ransomware and Mirai-scale outages.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames ransomware and consumer IoT abuse through a recurring fictional analyst, Sam, rather than a slide-only lecture. It opens with a bogus invoice email whose attachment is an HTML Application executed by the Windows scripting host, not a real document. Sam traces obfuscated script, recovers an XOR key from markers in the file, and uses injected alerts on a isolated machine to expose download URLs for encrypted payloads that only decrypt when the loader runs.

The storyline continues when Sam celebrates on social media and receives a malicious scalable vector graphic in a chat message, applies the same inspection habit, and lands on ransomware served from a relative’s desktop shortcut. The segment contrasts attacker polish—multilingual payment portals, captchas, tiered support—with sloppy claims such as labeling malware as safe, and notes selective “free” decryption that restores file metadata to hide an incomplete recovery.

A home-wide streaming outage then ties consumer risk to Mirai-style abuse of cameras and routers with default credentials, flooding DNS providers and recruiting bots in waves after source code leaks. The close urges changed passwords, segmentation, and turning off unneeded devices so personal hardware does not amplify attacks others feel as downtime.

talks.title: Breaking into the iCloud Keychain by: Vladimir Katalov
talks.teaser: Explains how forensic tools pull iCloud Keychain secrets from iPhones and linked accounts, and what protections limit that access.
talks.summary:
Vladimir Katalov opens with the problem facing phone examiners: chip-off extraction, which once worked on older devices, no longer yields usable data from iPhones because the storage is encrypted from the iPhone 4 onward. Much of the valuable material, including the keychain, has to be reached through other routes. He describes how synced data such as browsing history, bookmarks, open tabs and app data can be read from Apple's cloud service when an examiner holds valid account credentials, and how a list of devices tied to an account can be obtained.

The middle of the talk focuses on the keychain itself. Its items, which can include saved passwords, Wi-Fi network details, card numbers and authentication tokens, are protected by keys tied to the device and synchronised through an escrow-style service. Katalov walks through how two-factor authentication, a recovery code and token handling affect whether that data can be reached, and he shows a live demonstration of the process on an account. The details of the methods are described as they were presented, with a focus on what each protection changes.

He closes with practical guidance for account holders. Access to keychain data depends on the account's protections, so enabling two-factor authentication, using a strong password, and reviewing the devices linked to an account reduce exposure. For practitioners, the talk shows that the keychain's location in the cloud and its recovery design matter as much as the handset itself.

talks.title: Dissecting Exploit Kits by: Daniel Frank
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Dissecting Exploit Kits by: Daniel Frank.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk titled "Dissecting Exploit Kits," speaker Daniel Frank examines the operational workflow, architecture, and code execution patterns commonly found in web-based exploit kits. Exploit kits operate as automated attack frameworks designed to profile victim machines, deliver targeted exploits through browsers and plugins, and ultimately drop and execute malicious payloads.

### Key Topics
- **Exploit Kit Attack Chain**: The lifecycle begins with victim redirection to an exploit kit landing page (often via malicious servers or popups), followed by reconnaissance to profile installed software versions, targeted vulnerability exploitation, and payload execution.
- **Target Technologies & Vulnerabilities**: Exploit kits historically focused on widely deployed technologies such as Internet Explorer, Silverlight, and Adobe Flash. Frank references specific vulnerabilities, including CVE-2015-5119 (affecting Flash version 19 and earlier) and CVE-2016-0188.
- **Geographic Targeting**: Exploitation patterns and campaign telemetry show regional targeting tendencies, with high victim activity observed in countries such as Japan and South Korea.
- **Analyzed Exploit Kits**: The presentation provides detailed, stage-by-stage teardowns of two major exploit kits: Magnitude Exploit Kit and Sundown Exploit Kit.

### Technical Details
- **Magnitude Exploit Kit Walkthrough**:
  - **Stage 0 & Stage 1**: Begins with initial redirection and communication with malicious URLs. An obfuscated JavaScript stage profiles the client environment to confirm the presence of vulnerable configurations.
  - **Stage 2 (Exploitation)**: Exploits an issue within JavaScript parsing/JSON processing where nested fields lead to memory corruption or arbitrary execution. 
  - **Payload Deobfuscation & Execution**: The kit delivers an obfuscated payload (referenced in the code as `np90action`). A decoding function loops through character arrays, reassembles the binary data, and searches system processes to obtain execution handles. The downloaded payload is then written to disk and executed. The demonstration shows dropped malware—specifically ransomware—initiating file encryption on the host.
- **Sundown Exploit Kit Walkthrough**:
  - **Landing Page & Stages**: Features a simple landing page delivering multiple obfuscated payload objects. In Stage 1, scripts unpack base64 and byte-encoded strings to serve further exploit stages.
  - **Flash Weaponization**: Targets the client by loading multiple SWF/Flash files. The speaker extracts and deobfuscates a Flash payload by isolating an embedded decoding routine that reads the first byte as a XOR key to unpack compressed Flash binary data.
  - **Execution**: Once decompressed, the exploit retrieves the secondary binary payload, saves it into local application data folders (such as the APPDATA temp/bin paths), and spawns the malicious process.

### Takeaways
- Exploit kits heavily rely on layered multi-stage architectures (Stage 0 redirection, Stage 1 profiling, Stage 2 exploitation, and final payload staging) to complicate static analysis and evade automated detection.
- Threat actors utilize obfuscation techniques such as XOR encoding, character manipulation, and base64 layering within both JavaScript and Flash media.
- As modern browsers and platforms phased out legacy plugins like Flash and Silverlight, attackers shifted toward direct link distribution and alternative delivery mechanisms, though understanding exploit kit design remains critical for analyzing automated web exploitation.

talks.title: ROOTCON 10 Remote Code Execution via Java Native Deserialization by David Jorm
talks.teaser: Traces how Java deserialization flaws evolved from XML decoders to gadget chains that yield remote code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how Java deserialization has been used to reach remote code execution, moving from the built-in Java format to XML libraries. The speaker explains that an application deserializing attacker-controlled data can often be made to run code, then shows a live demo against an older REST framework that accepted XMLDecoder input and launched a calculator from a crafted document.

Next comes a timeline of cases. An XStream event handler class was used against Jenkins' XML API, and was later blacklisted. A 2013 incident combined a deserialization weakness with a file-path flaw in an upload class, letting an attacker write a JSP file into a web root. A 2011 finding showed a proxy-based handler could be triggered during deserialization, and Dozer, a type-mapping library, offered another route that remained unfixed for about two years. Around 2015, researchers showed that gadget chains built from common libraries such as Commons Collections could reach code execution on many Java servers, even without a vulnerable class in the application itself.

The closing point is that filtering known classes is a losing battle, and that the real problem is deserializing untrusted content at all. Practitioners should avoid deserializing untrusted input, keep readObject and readResolve logic free of risky behaviour, and treat class blacklists as stopgaps.

talks.title: ROOTCON 10 Big Data Analysis Applied to Network Security by Wilson Chua
talks.teaser: Shows how big data analytics on firewall, proxy and traffic logs can speed forensics and expose attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that big data analytics can help a stretched security team, since demand for skilled staff far outpaces the people being trained. The speaker outlines the core traits of big data, including volume, velocity and variety, and separates three levels of analysis: descriptive, predictive and prescriptive. These are presented as ways to do more with less.

Most of the talk is a series of field cases built on centralised firewall, proxy and traffic logs. A hosting client reported a slow website even though CPU and response-time graphs looked normal. Querying POST requests to the site over the previous week returned a ranked list of top source IPs within seconds, narrowing the suspects to one address. In another case, a treemap of aggregated traffic exposed an unusually small application cluster, and the client confirmed an old web application it no longer used; shutting it down reduced server load. Reconnaissance hunting searched for XML-RPC requests to surface brute-force sources. A bandwidth complaint was traced with packet-size histograms and port breakdowns to infected internal machines. Session counts below three were used to flag possible precursor attacks.

For the predictive part, the speaker trained a naive Bayes model in RapidMiner on labelled traffic. Accuracy fell sharply on a validation set, and reviewing the labels showed that some items marked as benign were actually malicious, where the model had been right. The practical takeaways are to start with simple fields such as packet size and session count, validate models on unseen data, and check labels before trusting them. Tools mentioned include Elastic, Splunk, Neo4j and RapidMiner.

talks.title: ROOTCON 10 ComeLEAK from Hacking to Behind Bars by godflux & XY
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss a national voter-records leak, how the data was pulled, and the arrest that followed.
talks.summary:
This session is a panel-style discussion built around a leak of voter records, referred to in the title as ComeLEAK. The panelists describe the data reportedly held in the leaked set, which they say covered about 55 million people and included names, birth dates, gender, civil status, birthplaces, disability status and voter identification numbers. They frame the incident as a story that runs from the intrusion to an arrest.

The panel walks through how the data was taken. According to the discussion, the attacker pulled the records in small increments rather than in one large transfer, so on the server side traffic would rise gradually and look like ordinary public interest in the election instead of an obvious breach. The suspect was later arrested, and the speakers note that he said he had no intention of selling the information to any political party.

The discussion then turns to whether the data should have been accessible at all. Panelists argue that personal records of this kind are not public simply because they can be queried, and that citizens hand over information on the understanding that the government will protect it. They describe the leak as a violation of public trust. The session closes with audience questions and a call for people to help their government protect citizens.

talks.title: ROOTCON 10 Halcyon by Sanoop Thomas
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of Halcyon, a Java IDE that simplifies writing, debugging, and exporting custom Nmap NSE scripts for faster scanning.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking how many attendees have used Nmap, then frames why custom Network Script Engine work matters when public script libraries lag behind new vulnerabilities or niche targets such as IoT. The speaker describes Halcyon as a Java-based IDE born from frustration with manual NSE authoring, positioned as a more approachable way to build scan logic than wrestling with raw script structure alone.

Halcyon is explained as condition-driven like Nmap itself, with templates per service, category selection, validation that surfaces mistakes, a port generator, and auto-generated boilerplate so repeated steps (fuzzing, spiders, and similar patterns) need less hand coding. The middle of the session is a live build of a script that calls an HTTP spider library, adjusts scan and debug settings, passes arguments, fixes a missing library import, and runs against a site to list discovered URLs. The speaker also shows exporting a finished script into the local Nmap script library and updating the database so future scans can reuse it.

Planned work includes richer reporting such as turning Nmap XML into CSV or Excel for pen-test deliverables, plus in-tool learning so developers are not forced to hunt documentation across the web. Practitioners should leave understanding that Halcyon targets faster turnaround for bespoke NSE checks when stock signatures are slow or absent, while still fitting the normal Nmap script workflow.

talks.title: ROOTCON 10 Reverse Engineering Swift Apps by Michael Gianarakis
talks.teaser: Shows how pentesters can reverse engineer compiled Swift iOS apps when source code isn't available.
talks.summary:
Michael Gianarakis explains why Swift is showing up more often in the mobile apps his team tests, and why that makes reversing harder than with Objective-C. Swift is a compiled language, and it is less dynamic than Objective-C, so the runtime tricks that work well on Objective-C apps give less back. The talk opens with a quick tour of the language's classes, initializers and methods, and shows how exported names change the way a method has to be called.

The middle of the talk moves to the compiled binary. Swift symbol names are mangled, and demangling them reveals modules, classes, functions, parameter and return types, with different output options giving more or less detail. Class dump style tools recover little from pure Swift classes, but classes that inherit from an Objective-C base expose much more. Scripts can rebuild a pseudo interface declaration from the output, and method names can sometimes be inferred from the naming conventions developers use when exported names are missing. Runtime inspection in a debugger works well for third-party apps, while scripted hooking is more fragile and can break on Swift-specific structures.

The closing point is that stripped binaries limit all of these techniques. Most serious issues in iOS assessments still come from design decisions, configuration and third-party frameworks rather than the language itself. Tooling is limited and Swift's syntax changes quickly, so testers should expect the methods to improve over time.

talks.title: ROOTCON 10 Shifting Paradigms from Windows to Mac by Nicholas Ramos and Michelle Morales
talks.teaser: Maps macOS internals, persistence tricks, landmark threats, and practical tools for analysts shifting from Windows malware work.
talks.summary:
Growing Mac adoption and thinner public documentation push many investigators who cut their teeth on Windows to learn how threats behave on Apple desktops. The opening frames macOS as a BSD- and NeXT-derived stack, notes steady platform changes such as dropping PowerPC and moving toward APFS, and argues that no operating system escapes malware pressure despite common user beliefs.

The core walks boot and persistence the way an analyst would: firmware and kernel touchpoints, kernel extension caches, LaunchDaemons and LaunchAgents, property lists in user and system folders, login items, and application hooks. It contrasts decentralized plist configuration with the Windows registry, explains Mach-O and fat binaries at a practical level, and points to plist and SQLite artifacts analysts should recognize. Apple controls such as Gatekeeper, XProtect, sandboxing, and code signing are described as real but bypassable layers rather than guarantees.

A second segment surveys notable Mac families—early viruses and worms, scareware and fake antivirus campaigns, firmware-resident Thunderstrike, and later commodity backdoors and ransomware such as KeRanger—and closes with command-line and GUI tooling for strings, disassembly, process inspection, persistence hunting, and network capture. The takeaway is that cross-platform Apple ecosystems will keep rewarding analysts who invest in Mac-specific file formats, startup mechanics, and hunting workflows.

talks.title: ROOTCON 10 Tranewreck by Jeff Kitson
talks.teaser: Traces Trane smart-thermostat research from tarball leaks through SMIL protocol abuse to vendor disclosure and assessment scripts.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes replacing a failed home furnace with a Trane package that required an XL850 ComfortLink thermostat. Curiosity about USB firmware updates led to downloading vendor source archives, extracting Ruby and BusyBox components, and mapping open network services including port 9999’s authentication challenge.

Source review surfaced hardcoded credentials, production keys, and a proprietary SMIL-style messaging layer that governs nearly every device function. By emulating the login handshake and issuing a broad subscribe command, an attacker can stream live sensor data and issue setpoints without meaningful rate limits—holding room temperature against user input and creating freeze or overheat risk. The same access exposes schedules, serial numbers, alarm history, and backbone connectivity details useful for impersonation or further attacks.

Disclosure involved Nexia and Trane/American Standard under Ingersoll Rand, with patches rolling over time but systemic issues such as weak update integrity and DNS trust remaining. The speaker releases Trainwreck tooling for passive discovery and active testing, notes similar devices in homes, corporate sites, and utilities, and urges auditors to mine public firmware tarballs for comparable flaws.
